scripts.opening:opening:
[mischievously] JAUNT: THE SCANDAL AT 1612 PRAIRIE. A Monday afternoon in November 1904, at the quiet north end of Prairie Avenue.

[short pause] Four stops along one short block. The house at 1612 has been a showplace for twenty years. [short pause] [dramatically] This year... it is a battlefield. A husband has gone to court, a judge has handed the house to the wife, [lowering voice] and in November the husband stood up in open court and said things about her that the whole city has now read in the Tribune. [short pause] [amused] The neighbours keep their curtains closed and their ears open.

[short pause] Start next door, where you can see the house the way it used to be.
scripts.stop:showplace: [warmly] 1608 Prairie, and beside it the big square house at 1612. Twenty years ago it belonged to a Studebaker, of the Studebaker Brothers carriage works, [proudly] and it was the brightest house on the street. In February 1884 some two hundred guests came here from a family wedding, and "The large residence was brilliantly illuminated, and every room was elaborately decorated with smilax and cut flowers." [short pause] A society column of 1887 noticed the traffic: "Morning and night, a showy turnout is noticed before the squarely-built house, with the number 1612 over the portals." A carriage-maker's house should have the finest carriages at its door, and it did. [long pause] [quietly] Look at it now. No turnout stands at the curb this afternoon. [whispers] A maid from next door is watching it from her steps. Walk to the gate of 1612.
scripts.stop:decree: [conspiratorially] 1612 Prairie. The Tribune has the story, and so does everybody else. [short pause] Last May the husband, Charles E. Brown, filed a bill for divorce. His wife Catherine is 27, "the daughter of Gen. Graves, a wealthy resident of Buffalo". [lowering voice] The grounds were "Habitual drunkenness and statutory charges". [short pause] [surprised] Then Judge Tuley gave Mrs. Brown possession of this house, where she and her husband and their son had lived, and $200 a month while the suit was pending. [amused] So the wife holds the fortress and the husband is outside it. [short pause] [softly] Behind those windows live a woman the papers have made famous and a small boy. The house will stand until it is razed circa 1960. [short pause] Step next door and hear what the husband said in November.
scripts.stop:charges: [amused] 1616 Prairie, the next door south, where the neighbours read the Tribune with their coffee. [short pause] [dramatically] In November Mr. Brown went back to court and charged that his wife "had conducted herself in a disgraceful manner, had been habitually intoxicated, and had done many freakish things, [incredulous] such as playing a violin in a broken automobile while a man pushed the machine along a public highway, [laughs] and dancing about the rear of their home clothed only in a nightrobe." [short pause] [lowering voice] There was more. He named a man: "E. C. Edsall, an automobile salesman." With Edsall, the husband charged, she ran off to an eastern summer resort and later to New York City. [mischievously] It is the most delicious scandal on Prairie Avenue in years, and two maids on these steps are making the most of it. [long pause] [serious] But a divorce is not only about two people. [softly] Look for the boy.
scripts.stop:boy: [gently] Across the street at 1613, look back at the west side of the block. [short pause] The boy is Charles Edward Brown, the couple's only son, and he is the real prize in this fight. A nurse walks him along the sidewalk past his own front door; his mother has the house, and his father wants it back, and wants him. [short pause] The court has not decided. In the newspapers he is a line at the end of every story. [short pause] [tenderly] On this walk he is the only person in the whole affair who has done nothing at all. The Tribune will report the end of it in March 1905. [short pause] [quietly] By then the house, the boy and the woman will each have gone a different way.
scripts.ending:march: [measured] End of the walk. After a bitter fight, early in 1905, [short pause] the husband won: the divorce, the house on Prairie Avenue and the custody of the boy. On 8 March 1905 he sold the house to Charles Palmerston Anderson, the Episcopal bishop of Chicago. [short pause] [darkly] That same week the Tribune found Catherine Brown in a police cell, arrested at 3667 Wabash Avenue, where the police said she had been living as Kittie Casey, and fined $85. [sadly] "I am penniless," she said. "I cannot pay the fine." [short pause] In her cell she said: "It's all because a woman is jealous of me, I guess." [long pause] [softly] The general's daughter from Buffalo had held 1612 Prairie for less than a year.
